passage: Afreen typed, "Write a poem about rain," and the assistant produced eight neat lines in seconds. She gasped. "It's like magic!" she told her father, Kamal. Then she asked how tall the tallest tree is and copied the confident answer straight into her science page. The next day a classmate showed her a book with a different number. Afreen's cheeks warmed; she had believed it only because it sounded so sure. From then on she checked important facts in a book too. Kamal, who had seen her typing late, asked, "Can I see what you're chatting about?" Afreen felt watched and stiffened, but she turned the screen and explained she used it for poems and facts. They agreed on a rule: chats only at the kitchen table, with the door open. When Ms. Amandeep asked whether anyone had used an AI for the poem project, Afreen's mouth went dry and part of her wanted to say no. Instead she said, "I asked it for an idea, then wrote my own lines about my grandmother's kitchen in the monsoon." Ms. Amandeep smiled, read the lines and suggested a stronger last line, which Afreen wrote herself.

qa.q: How many lines did the assistant write for the rain poem?
qa.a: It produced eight neat lines.

qa.q: How did Afreen's early trust in the assistant differ from what she did after her classmate showed her the book?
qa.a: At first she believed the confident answer about the tallest tree and copied it, but after the book showed a different number she checked important facts in a book too, learning that a sure-sounding answer can be wrong.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when her mouth went dry as the teacher asked about AI?
qa.a: She felt nervous and tempted to say no, worried about what the teacher would think.

qa.q: What could Afreen do next to keep her poems her own?
qa.a: She could use the assistant only for ideas, write her own lines from her own memories and keep telling her teacher how she used it.

grounding: A child meets an AI assistant with awe, then over-trust, then a parent's worry and a teacher's question, and learns to check facts and be honest.

passage: Nilesh was brushing his teeth when an old memory played again: at twenty he had put his name alone on a group design, and a teammate had lost her chance at an internship. Six years on, his stomach still turned. He finally wrote her a message saying what he had done, that he was sorry, and offering to email her old professor with the truth. She replied kindly. After that, whenever the memory came back, he reminded himself that he had made it right and now shared credit openly. On Sunday he drove to see his father, Manoj, who had worked two jobs when Nilesh was small and rarely made it to school events. Nilesh saw that Manoj had been young and scared then. He said, "Thank you for working so hard. I still need you to stop asking about my salary." Manoj nodded, a little embarrassed. On the drive home Nilesh replayed how Tanuja, a former classmate, had mocked his accent at a wedding last year. His jaw clenched. He talked it over with a friend at dinner, then wrote down what he needed: to stop rehearsing replies. He deleted the draft message to Tanuja and went for a walk, feeling lighter, though no apology had come.

qa.q: What did Nilesh offer to do for his old teammate?
qa.a: He offered to email her old professor with the truth.

qa.q: How did Nilesh's response to his own old mistake differ from what he did about Tanuja's mocking?
qa.a: For his own mistake Nilesh wrote a message saying what he had done, said he was sorry and offered to email her old professor, then reminded himself he had made it right; for Tanuja's mocking, when no apology had come, he talked it over with a friend, wrote down what he needed and went for a walk feeling lighter.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling when the old memory came back while he brushed his teeth?
qa.a: He felt guilty, since his stomach still turned six years later.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do next with his father?
qa.a: He could keep his boundary about salary questions while thanking Manoj for the effort he made.

grounding: A young adult forgives himself after making amends, forgives a parent's limits while keeping a boundary, and releases resentment toward someone who never apologised.

passage: Ira's charts were the best in the group, and when she presented them Anand felt a sour twist. He had almost hidden his own rough draft until he asked her how she chose the colours; she showed him in five minutes, and he finished his section properly. In the meeting, Anand and Salma disagreed hotly: he wanted a survey, she wanted interviews. They agreed to test both on ten respondents each, and when the data favoured interviews and the group voted for that plan, Anand nodded and kept working without sulking. He handed Salma the results table and said, "Can you show me a draft on Wednesday and again on Friday?" When the draft arrived he said, "The layout is clear. The second column needs labels." On the last night the library closed at nine, so they moved to a canteen table, and Salma stayed until midnight helping him fix his broken references. Anand said, "You saved my grade. Thank you, truly. Send me your slides on Monday." On Monday he formatted her section without being asked.

qa.q: How many respondents did the group test each method on?
qa.a: They tested both methods on ten respondents each.

qa.q: How did Anand's reaction to Ira's charts differ from his reaction when the data favoured Salma's plan?
qa.a: With Ira's charts he felt a sour twist of envy but chose to learn from her instead of hiding his work; when the data favoured interviews and the group voted, he accepted the decision and kept working without sulking.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when Ira presented her charts?
qa.a: He felt envious, a sour twist, because her work was better than his.

qa.q: What could Anand do next to return Salma's help?
qa.a: He could offer her help in return, as he did by formatting her section, and keep thanking her for staying late.

grounding: Four moments in one student group project show envy of a star, a disagreement settled by data, hand-over with checkpoints and gratitude for late help.

passage: Three friends met for coffee on Sunday, each carrying a different piece of a relationship. Pema said quietly that her partner had said he would leave if she kept saying no to something private, and had called her cold in front of a friend. She felt afraid and confused. "That's not love, and it isn't your fault," said Harsha, and Sumit offered to go with her to a counsellor. Before they left the cafe, the three of them rang the counselling centre and booked a slot for that week, and Pema decided to keep her boundary. Harsha told them how, the night before, he had wanted closeness with his wife, who was tired and unsure. He asked, listened when she said not tonight, made her tea, and did not sulk. Sumit admitted he loved his partner deeply but had gone weeks without saying it. That night he left a note on the mirror and cooked her favourite dal. After dinner he told her about a shame from his teens that he had never shared. He watched her face, and she squeezed his hand and thanked him for telling her.

qa.q: Who offered to go with Pema to a counsellor?
qa.a: Sumit offered to go with Pema to a counsellor.

qa.q: How did Harsha's response to his wife's answer differ from the way Pema's partner reacted to her no?
qa.a: Harsha asked, listened when she said not tonight, made tea and did not sulk, while Pema's partner said he would leave and called her cold to get his way, which is not love.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling when she talked about her partner's threat to leave?
qa.a: She felt afraid and confused, unsure what was happening but still holding her boundary.

qa.q: How could Sumit keep showing love in the daily routine?
qa.a: He could keep giving small regular attention, thanks and notes, like the mirror note and her favourite dal, instead of waiting for a grand gesture.

grounding: Three friends share four parts of intimacy: a partner who pressures with threats, a respectful listening to no, small daily affection and slow sharing of a shame.

passage: At the playgroup, Aditi's mother Vinita crouched and said, "Mama goes to buy milk, and I come back after snack." She waved from the door and did not sneak away. Aditi wailed for a moment, then picked up a wooden duck and returned to the sand tray. When a new volunteer sat down, Aditi edged behind Vinita's knee and stared, and only took a block once Vinita chatted easily and laughed with the volunteer. Nearby, Tejas's mother arrived late, and Tejas hit her arm and turned his back. She knelt and said, "You got very upset when Mama left the room. I'm back now." Tejas wept, then climbed into her lap. In the corner sat Zayn, who no longer cried when his caregiver left. He played silently with a spoon, flat and still, and grown-ups often remarked what a good boy he was. The playgroup leader noticed, sat beside him, spoke softly and offered a lap. That same afternoon the leader shared what they had seen with the centre's child welfare worker, so that someone could gently check in with Zayn's family.

qa.q: What did Aditi pick up after her brief wail?
qa.a: Aditi picked up a wooden duck.

qa.q: How did Aditi's goodbye differ from Zayn's silence, and what did each show about what the children had learned?
qa.a: Aditi's mother said a clear goodbye, waved from the door and came back after snack, so Aditi wailed for a moment and returned to the sand tray; Zayn no longer cried when his caregiver left and played silently, flat and still, which looks like being good but suggests his crying had brought no comfort.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when he hit his mother's arm and turned his back?
qa.a: He felt upset and angry, the fear of being left turned into fury.

qa.q: How could Tejas's mother respond so that he does not learn to hide his needs?
qa.a: She could keep welcoming him calmly and naming the feeling, as she did, rather than punishing the anger.

grounding: Four toddlers meet a caregiver leaving: brief protest from secure trust, anger on return, flat silence after unanswered need and wariness of a stranger.

passage: Raghav flicked rules away like dust. "Babies," he said to Chinmay, who had refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets. Omkar's stomach clenched. He had gone along the week before, laughing at the wrong moment because he feared being left out. This time he said quietly to Chinmay at the bike stand, "Can I say no with you?" Chinmay grinned. "Sure. Just say, not today, I've got homework. Keep it short." When Raghav sneered, Omkar used exactly those words, and Chinmay added, "Come for chai after school, though." Nobody lectured Raghav, and he shrugged. The next day Ma'am asked where Raghav had been. Omkar started to say, "He was sick," then stopped: Raghav had told them he had tried a stunt on a wall and hurt his wrist. Omkar told Raghav, "I'm not going to lie for you, but I care what happens to you. Show your wrist to the nurse." Raghav went. That afternoon Omkar told the class teacher what he knew, without mocking anyone.

qa.q: What did Chinmay refuse to do?
qa.a: Chinmay refused to bunk the last period and ride bikes on the highway without helmets.

qa.q: How did Omkar's earlier going along differ from his later refusal, and what did Chinmay's example add?
qa.a: Earlier Omkar laughed along because he feared being left out; later he refused with an ally and a short reply, and Chinmay stayed friendly without lecturing, which made saying no easier.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Raghav called Chinmay a baby?
qa.a: His stomach clenched, so he felt afraid of being laughed at or left out.

qa.q: What did Omkar do about Raghav's hurt wrist, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He refused to lie for Raghav, urged him to see the nurse and told the class teacher, showing loyalty to Raghav's wellbeing rather than to the risky stunt.

grounding: Four teenagers meet peer pressure to bunk and take risks: contempt for rule-followers, going along from fear, covering for a friend and a friend who refuses and is followed.
